```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_pdftools <- requireNamespace("pdftools", quietly = TRUE)
```

Before a model can read a document, the text has to come out of the file. That
step, *ingestion*, is easy to overlook and hard to undo. Text lost here, or
damaged by too much clean-up, is text no model will see, however good the rest
of the pipeline is. This guide covers what harnessr can read, what it keeps, what
it removes, and how to check a folder before spending anything on it.

`vignette("harnessr")` introduces the package and the ideas used here.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE)
```

## What ingestion produces

`gr_ingest()` reads a file and returns a *document*: the text split into
*blocks*, which are the paragraphs, headings and list items as the file has them.
harnessr includes a short example, an annual report written in Markdown:

```{r}
doc <- gr_ingest(gr_example())
doc
```

Each block records where it came from: the page, for formats that have pages,
and the section heading it sits under:

```{r}
doc$blocks[1:6, c("block_id", "page", "section", "kind")]
```

This *provenance* is what lets an answer point back to where it came from:
`ans$evidence` reports the page and section of every chunk an answer rests on.
`page` is `NA` here because Markdown has no pages; a PDF fills it in.

`doc$text` is all the blocks joined, and `doc$stats` summarises the document:

```{r}
unlist(doc$stats[c("blocks", "chars", "tokens", "chars_removed")])
```

You rarely need to call `gr_ingest()` yourself, since `answer_document()` does it
for you. Calling it directly shows you what the model will get.

## What harnessr can read

Each file type is handled by an *extractor*, chosen by the file's extension.
`available` says whether the packages it needs are installed:

```{r}
gr_extractors()[, c("name", "extensions", "available")]
```

| extractor | what it keeps | needs |
|---|---|---|
| `txt` | paragraphs, split at blank lines | nothing |
| `md` | paragraphs, plus headings as sections and code blocks and tables marked as such | nothing |
| `html` | text inside `<h1>` to `<h4>`, `<p>`, `<li>`, `<td>`, `<pre>` and `<blockquote>`; text anywhere else (a bare `<div>`, `<h5>`, `<th>`) is dropped, as are scripts, styles, navigation bars and footers | `xml2` |
| `docx` | paragraphs, with headings as sections in any interface language; each table row as one block, its cells joined by a vertical bar; footnotes and endnotes after the paragraph that cites them; images inside the file are read by OCR when `tesseract` is installed | `xml2` |
| `pdf` | the text of each page in reading order, with its page number and headings as sections; pages with no text are read by OCR | `pdftools` (and `tesseract` and `magick` for OCR) |
| `image` | the text in a picture, by OCR | `tesseract` |

A file whose extension no extractor claims, such as an old `.doc` or a
spreadsheet, is not read. `gr_inventory()`, below, finds those before a run
rather than during one.

You can also pass text directly. A string that is not the path of an existing
file is read as the document itself:

```{r}
memo <- gr_ingest("Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.\n\nHeadcount grew to 1,204.")
memo$blocks[, c("block_id", "text")]
```

The exception is a string that ends in an extension some extractor claims but
names no file. That is an error:

```{r error = TRUE}
gr_ingest("anual-report.pdf")
```

Any other string is read as text, including a path whose extension is mistyped
or is one no extractor claims. A string that looks like a path (it has a `/` and
an extension) also raises a warning, since the answer that follows would be
about a file name:

```{r}
typo <- gr_ingest("reports/2024/annual-report.pfd")
typo$text
typo$source
```

`source` is how to tell the two apart: it holds the path when a file was read,
and `<inline text>` when the string itself was.

A web address is downloaded and read with the extractor for what the server
sent back: a specific type it declares, else the extension in the address, else
the first bytes of the file, which settle a PDF, a Word file or an HTML page
however they were labelled. A download no extractor reads is refused rather
than read as text. `source` holds the address, and a download that fails is an
error that says why:

```{r eval = FALSE}
doc <- gr_ingest("https://example.org/reports/annual-report-2024.pdf")
doc$source
#> [1] "https://example.org/reports/annual-report-2024.pdf"
```

Within a session an address is downloaded once; the next read of it comes from
the cache, as a file does.

## Sections and headings

For Markdown, HTML, Word and PDF files, each block records the heading it falls
under (the next section says how a PDF's headings are found). The example report
has these sections:

```{r}
unique(doc$blocks$section)
```

Sections matter later. The `structural` way of cutting a document into chunks
never lets a chunk straddle two sections (`vignette("segment")`), and the
`preview` reading strategy plans its reading section by section. A plain text
file has no headings, so its blocks have no section.

## PDFs

A PDF is read page by page, and every block carries its page number. That is what
lets a quotation be traced to "page 12" rather than to "somewhere in the file".

```{r eval = has_pdftools}
pdf_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".pdf")
grDevices::pdf(pdf_file, width = 8.5, height = 11)
for (page in list(c("Summary", "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024."),
                  c("Outlook", "The board expects revenue of 50 million dollars in 2025."))) {
  graphics::plot.new()
  graphics::text(0, c(0.95, 0.9), page, adj = 0)
}
invisible(grDevices::dev.off())

report <- gr_ingest(pdf_file)
report$blocks[, c("page", "section", "kind", "text")]
```

A PDF's text comes out as the page looks, which is not always the order a person
reads in, so harnessr puts it back in reading order:

- A page set in two columns is read one column after the other. Without this,
  each line would join the start of a line from each column.
- Running heads and feet (short lines repeated at the top or bottom of many
  pages, such as a journal name or "Page 3 of 12") are removed.
- Headings are found, so blocks carry sections as they do for Markdown and
  Word. They come from the PDF's bookmarks when it has them. Otherwise a line
  that is only a standard section name ("Introduction", "2. Methods",
  "Results") counts. That is how "Summary" was found above; "Outlook" is not a
  standard name, so it stayed text.

`gr_ingest_spec(layout = "raw")` turns all three off and keeps each page as it
is laid out. Footnotes, tables and pages in three or more columns can still come
out in an order that reads oddly, so check a few pages of `report$text` before
relying on a new kind of PDF.

## Scanned pages and OCR

A scanned PDF is a picture of text, with no text inside it to extract. Reading it
needs *optical character recognition* (OCR), which turns the picture back into
text. OCR is slow (seconds per page) and never perfect, so harnessr uses it only
where it is needed:

```{r eval = FALSE}
# The default: OCR any page with fewer than 40 characters of text.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "auto"))

# A page with a little text but mostly scanned content: raise the threshold.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "auto", ocr_min_chars = 200))

# Everything, or nothing.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "always"))
gr_ingest("born-digital.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "never"))

# Another language, at a higher resolution.
gr_ingest("scan.pdf", gr_ingest_spec(ocr_lang = "deu", ocr_dpi = 400))
```

OCR on PDFs needs both `tesseract` and `magick`. Without them a scanned page
comes back nearly empty and harnessr warns (`gr_ocr_unavailable`). The document
lists those pages in `doc$stats$unread_pages`, and an answer drawn from it is
marked partial. The same holds with `ocr = "never"`: a page with no text, or
only a stamp or a running head, is listed as unread. A document with too little
text left is refused outright, as the next section shows. The `"scanned"` recipe
is set up for this kind of document.

## Cleaning

Extracted text is rarely clean. PDFs break words across lines with hyphens, repeat
the page number on every page, and use typographic ligatures ("ﬁ" for "fi").
harnessr tidies this with *cleaners*. Each does one job and can be turned on or
off:

```{r}
gr_cleaners()[, c("name", "stage", "default_on")]
```

The five marked `default_on` run unless you say otherwise. The ones below are off
by default, for these reasons:

- `remove_numbers` replaces every digit with a space, which makes any question
  about a figure, date or percentage unanswerable.
- `captions` removes lines that look like figure and table captions, which
  destroys documents made mostly of tables.
- `urls` and `emails` remove links and addresses, which are sometimes the answer.
- `references` cuts everything from a line reading just "References",
  "Bibliography" or "Works cited" to the end of the document, when that line
  starts at or after 40% of the text, so a table of contents near the start
  does not cut the document. The line may be numbered ("7. References") or a
  Markdown heading ("## References"); a line inside a fenced code block is
  not a heading. `cleaner_opts = list(references_after = )`
  moves that share, a number from 0 to 1. The cut loses the reference list if
  your question is about the sources.

Cleaning cannot be undone later: no reader can recover what it removes. Know
what each choice costs before you make it.

### Presets

Instead of naming cleaners one by one, use a *preset*:

| preset | what it runs |
|---|---|
| `"none"` | nothing |
| `"minimal"` | control characters and whitespace only |
| `"standard"` | the default: page numbers, broken hyphens, control characters, ligatures, whitespace |
| `"academic"` | standard, plus `captions` and `references` |
| `"scan"` | standard, plus repeated page headers and footers |
| `"legacy"` | what the first version of this package did, number stripping included; for comparison only |

Here is how much text each leaves of the example report:

```{r}
presets <- c("none", "minimal", "standard", "academic", "scan", "legacy")
vapply(presets, function(p) gr_ingest(gr_example(), gr_ingest_spec(clean = p))$stats$chars,
       integer(1))
```

Or name the cleaners yourself:

```{r}
tidy <- gr_ingest(gr_example(),
                  gr_ingest_spec(clean = c("page_numbers", "hyphenation", "collapse_whitespace")))
tidy$stats$chars
```

### Seeing what cleaning removed

Every document records what each cleaner took out, in characters:

```{r}
vapply(doc$stats$clean_log, function(step) step$chars_removed, integer(1))
```

A negative number means a cleaner added characters, for example by expanding
"ﬁ" to "fi". If a cleaner removed far more than you expected, turn it off and
compare.

`gr_clean()` runs cleaners on any text, so you can try a configuration on a few of
your own lines first. Cleaners always run in two stages, `early` before `late`,
whatever order you list them in; otherwise number removal would strip the "1"
from "Page 1" before the page-number cleaner could recognise the line:

```{r}
cleaned <- gr_clean(c("Page 1", "Revenue rose to 45.2 million in 2024."),
                    steps = c("remove_numbers", "page_numbers"))
as.character(cleaned)
```

The second line shows why `remove_numbers` is off by default.

## When too little text is left

A document with almost no text after cleaning (a scan read without OCR, an empty
file, a PDF of images) is refused rather than sent to the model. A model shown
nothing would answer "not in the document" for a document that may well contain
the answer:

```{r error = TRUE}
gr_ingest("Tiny.")
```

The limit is `min_chars` (20 characters by default) in `gr_ingest_spec()`.

## Reading the same file twice

Ingestion is cached for the rest of the R session. Asking a second question of the
same file, or trying a different way of cutting it into chunks, reuses the
extracted text instead of reading the file again. The cache notices when the file
changes (its size or modification time) and when any ingestion setting changes.
Turn it off with `gr_options(cache_documents = FALSE)`.

## Before reading a whole folder

A folder of documents hides problems that a single file makes obvious: a few old
`.doc` files nobody can read, scanned PDFs without text, an empty file, or a
subfolder you forgot about. `gr_inventory()` finds all of these in seconds,
without calling a model and without an API key:

```{r}
inbox <- file.path(tempdir(), "inbox")
dir.create(inbox, showWarnings = FALSE)
invisible(file.copy(gr_example(), file.path(inbox, "annual_report.md"),
                    overwrite = TRUE))
writeLines("Headcount grew to 1,204 employees across nine sites.",
           file.path(inbox, "notes.txt"))
writeLines("(a Word 97 document)", file.path(inbox, "minutes.doc"))
invisible(file.create(file.path(inbox, "empty.txt")))

inv <- gr_inventory(inbox)
inv
```

It lists every file, including the ones that will not be read, because "one file
will be skipped" is exactly what you need to know before the run:

```{r}
inv$files[, c("file", "extractor", "status", "tokens")]
```

The statuses:

| status | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ready` | an extractor can read it, and there is text |
| `needs_ocr` | a PDF whose pages have no text; it needs OCR |
| `needs_package` | an extractor can read it, but its package is not installed |
| `no_extractor` | no extractor reads this kind of file |
| `empty` | nothing to read |
| `unreadable` | it could not be opened; `note` says why |

It shows three things a corpus run would otherwise hide:

| what it shows | why it matters |
|---|---|
| files no extractor claims | they were dropped without appearing anywhere, so a folder of `.doc` files read as an empty corpus |
| PDFs with no text layer | they extract to nothing, then answer `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT`, which looks the same as a document that does not say |
| files in subfolders | they are listed with their `folder`, so a subfolder you forgot is visible; `recursive = FALSE` scans one level only |

`folder` is a column, so `split(inv$files, inv$files$folder)` gives you the
piles. `gr_inventory()` does not choose a recipe for you. A router that quietly
reads one document with `retrieve` and another with `stuff` hands you a
plausible answer built on part of a file with nothing saying so. It also makes
`gr_compare()` meaningless, because the corpus no longer had one configuration.
Group the rows yourself and pass each group the recipe you picked; reading a
whole folder is in `vignette("review")`.

`inv$totals` adds up the tokens and prices one request per readable file with
your model: its tokens in, and an assumed 500-token answer out. Treat
`cost_floor_usd` as a rough guide rather than a bound. Reading strategies that
make several requests per document cost more, and short answers cost less.
Files whose size is unknown until they are read by OCR are not in the total;
`tokens_unknown` counts them.

```{r}
unlist(inv$totals[c("readable", "tokens", "cost_floor_usd")])
```

## Choosing the settings

Two groups of ingest settings change what the model is given: cleaning and OCR.
Each walkthrough below says what the setting controls and what it trades off,
the signs in your results that point to changing it, where its default came
from, and how to test a change. `vignette("settings")` lists every ingest
setting with its default.

The tests use `hr_sweep()`, which builds one arm per value of a setting, and
`hr_benchmark()`, which runs every arm on a reference of questions. Here they
run on one question and a stand-in model that always gives the right answer,
so they show how a sweep is built and read, not which value is better.
`vignette("compare")` runs sweeps on a reference with dev and test splits and
reads them with intervals.

```{r}
qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
says <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
```

### Cleaning presets and `references_after` {#set-clean}

**What it controls.** `clean` chooses the cleaners that run on the extracted
text, by preset or by name (see "Presets" above), and
`cleaner_opts = list(references_after = )` sets where the `references`
cleaner may cut. Cleaning trades noise against loss: page numbers, running
heads and captions cost tokens and can mislead retrieval, but a cleaner that
removes too much removes it for good, and no later setting can bring it back.

**Signs it needs changing.** An answer of `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` for a fact you can
see in the file, or a quotation that fails verification, can mean a cleaner
removed the text; look in `doc$stats$clean_log` for a cleaner that removed far
more than the others. Answers that quote page headers or figure captions as if
they were findings point the other way, to `"academic"` or `"scan"`. Under
`"academic"`, an answer about a paper's sources that says they are not in the
document means the reference list was cut. A document whose table of contents
has a "References" line after the first 40% of its text is cut there; raise
`references_after` for such documents.

**Where the defaults came from.** `"standard"` was chosen as the preset for
born-digital text and has not been compared with the others. `references_after`
is 0.4, set when the cleaner was written. Both are `untested` in
`gr_settings_table("ingest")`.

**How to test it.** Sweep the presets and look at what was sent:

```{r}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("fast"), list(clean = c("standard", "academic", "scan", "none")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = says, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.clean, bench, mean)
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

On the example report, `"academic"` sends 62 fewer prompt tokens than
`"standard"`, because it drops the caption lines and the reference list after
the `## References` heading, and `"none"` sends 8 more.
`hr_sweep_check()` finds that `"scan"` sent exactly the requests `"standard"`
sent: the example has no running heads, so on it that comparison would measure
nothing but run-to-run spread. The same check tells you whether a
`references_after` sweep reaches your documents at all:

```{r}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("fast", list(clean = "academic")),
                 data.frame(cleaner_opts = I(list(list(references_after = 0.4),
                                                  list(references_after = 0.8)))))
hr_sweep_check(hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = says, split = "dev",
                            scorer = gr_scorer_answer()))
```

Both values sent the same requests. The example report's `## References`
heading starts 94% of the way through its text, after both 40% and 80%, so
both values cut the text at the same line. A `references_after` sweep changes
what is sent only for a document whose heading falls between the two values.
Run it on your own documents, with questions whose answers sit near the end.

### OCR settings {#set-ocr}

**What it controls.** `ocr` decides which pages are read as pictures:
`"auto"` reads a page by OCR only when it has fewer than `ocr_min_chars`
characters of text (40), `"always"` reads every page that way and `"never"`
none. `ocr_trigger` says which text those characters are counted on:
`"raw_text"` counts the page's whole text layer, and `"after_running_lines"`
counts what is left once the running heads, feet and stamps the layout pass
drops are taken out. `ocr_dpi` is the resolution the page is rendered at, and
`ocr_lang` the Tesseract language. OCR costs seconds per page and adds
recognition errors; not running it on a scanned page leaves that page empty.
The blocks of a page OCR read have `kind = "ocr"` (its headings keep
`"heading"`) and carry `ocr_confidence`, Tesseract's mean word confidence for
the page, from 0 to 100.

**Signs it needs changing.** `doc$stats$unread_pages` lists pages that came
back empty, and an answer from such a document is marked partial. A scanned
page with a printed header or stamp can carry more than 40 characters of text
and so skip OCR under `"auto"`: set `ocr_trigger = "after_running_lines"`
when the stamp repeats on every page, or raise `ocr_min_chars` when it does
not. A low `ocr_confidence` on the blocks an answer cites says to read that
page by hand. Misread numbers or
letters in OCR text (a quotation that fails verification against a page that
plainly says it) point to a higher `ocr_dpi` or the right `ocr_lang`.

**Where the defaults came from.** `ocr_dpi = 300` follows Tesseract's
documentation on improving output quality (`cited`). `ocr = "auto"` runs OCR
only where a page has no text layer, and no other choice has been compared.
`ocr_min_chars = 40` was set when OCR was added and has not been tuned, and
`ocr_lang = "eng"` is English because the package's own examples are in
English. `ocr_trigger = "raw_text"` is how pages were chosen before the
setting existed, and has not been compared with `"after_running_lines"`. All
four are `untested`.

**How to test it.** OCR needs a scanned file and the tesseract and magick
packages, so this runs on your own documents, with a reference built from them
by `gr_qa_reference()` and your own client:

```{r eval = FALSE}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("scanned"), list(ocr_min_chars = c(40, 200, 1000)))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_reference, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(correct ~ param.ocr_min_chars, bench, mean)
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

A row from `hr_sweep_check()` means no page crossed the threshold between the
two values, so they read the documents the same way.

`ocr_trigger` is swept the same way, and decides which pages are read before
any request, so `doc$stats$unread_pages` and the `"ocr"` blocks of each
ingestion show its effect for nothing:

```{r eval = FALSE}
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("scanned"),
                 list(ocr_trigger = c("raw_text", "after_running_lines")))
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, my_reference, runs = 5, client = my_client, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(correct ~ param.ocr_trigger, bench, mean)
```

## Adding your own

A format harnessr does not know, or a clean-up step your documents need, can be
added and then used exactly like a built-in one. A cleaner that drops lines
marked "CONFIDENTIAL":

```{r}
gr_register_cleaner("drop_confidential", stage = "early",
  fn = function(x, opts) gsub("(?mi)^\\s*CONFIDENTIAL.*$", "", x, perl = TRUE),
  description = "Remove lines marked CONFIDENTIAL")

gr_ingest("CONFIDENTIAL - internal only\n\nRevenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.",
          gr_ingest_spec(clean = c("drop_confidential", "collapse_whitespace")))$text
```

`?gr_register_extractor` shows how to add a file format, and
`vignette("extending")` covers every kind of addition.

```{r include = FALSE}
gr_options(old)
```

## Next

Once the text is out, the next decisions are how to cut it into chunks,
covered in `vignette("segment")`, and how the model should read them, covered
in `vignette("readers")`. To read a whole folder once `gr_inventory()` has
checked it, see `vignette("review")`.
